Wikipedia has a pretty good answer:

Since the Copyright Act of 1909, United States musicians have had the right to record a version of someone else's previously recorded and released tune, whether its music alone or music with lyrics. A license can be negotiated between representatives of the interpreting artist and the copyright holder, or recording published tunes can fall under a mechanical license whereby the recording artist pays a standard royalty to the original author/copyright holder through an organization such as the Harry Fox Agency, and is safe under copyright law even if they do not have any permission from the original author. A similar service was provided by Limelight by RightsFlow, until January, 2015 when they announced they will be closing their service. The U.S. Congress introduced the mechanical license to head off an attempt by the Aeolian Company to monopolize the piano roll market.

Although a composer cannot deny anyone a mechanical license for a new recorded version, the composer has the right to decide who will release the first recording of a song. Bob Dylan took advantage of this right when he refused his own record company the right to release a live recording of "Mr. Tambourine Man."

Live performances of copyrighted songs are typically arranged through performing rights organizations such as ASCAP or BMI.

I'm looking to buy a 30-06 rifle for hunting for under 1k. I'm not a pro so im getting overwhelmed by all the options. Any recommendations for a no nonsense solid rifle?

I don't have much experience with 30-06 rifles, but I remember when I was learning to shoot long-distance I used one that belonged to my uncle. I'm not exactly sure of the model number but I think it was the CZ-557 Synthetic, I found it to be really nice to shoot, pretty accurate, and my uncle has been using it as his main hunting rifle for years now without complaint. Honestly, in my experience you can't go wrong with a CZ for cheap and reliable.

Honestly the best value for your money is to go used, check out local gun shops and pawn shops, quality used bolt guns are plentiful in most places. Any cash saved on the gun can be directed at things like optics and ammo. Realistically any of the big name bolt guns should do the job, my personal preference would be a Ruger model 77, but a used Savage 110, Remington 700 or Winchester 70 are good rifles for less dollars than buying new.

I agree with the used purchase but I'm going to add auto loaders to the mix. My all time Favorite hunting rifle was a Remington 742 (Woodmaster). Any woodmaster Manufactured prior to 2007 would be a nice hunting rifle. The beauty of Hunting rifles is that most people don't shoot them Much.

IMHO 30-06 is the finest round for hunting White Tail, Mule Deer, Elk and Antelope. I've had several manufactures' 30-06 rifles but my favorite is my Ruger 77 Stainless Steel with Composite Stock. Mounted is a Leopold 3 x 9. Scored 2 B&C White Tails, one at 310 yards with my Ruger. Lot of folks swear by .270 and .308 but 30-06 has been around for a lot of years and ammo (including hunting rounds) can be easily found and not too expensive.

Be classy and find a decent 1903 Springfield. If you want optics, there are plenty of sporterized ones out there setup for scopes. If you don't want optics find one all military original or as close as you can get, and enjoy a classic American rifle.
Savage has a 111 combo with a Nikon 3-9x40 BDC out right now that retails new for 580. They go on sale frequently and have rebates from time to time as well. That gives you plenty left over for ammo.
Tikka is nice, Rem 700 is living off of it's previously well earned reputation but no longer worth the cost. Savage is also nice.

I know there's a lot of Freedom Group hate but I found a Remington 783 for $230 New in 30-06 on GunBroker. Its a very decent gun I can shoot less than 1moa or less at 200 yards with it. There are many other and better rifles especially with your budget but I saved that money for some great rings and a good scope. And lots of ammo. 30-06 is an expensive round. If you don't reload, go to a gun show and make friends with someone who sells reloads. You'll get great inexpensive ammo and you can trade in your brass for precision cheap reloads.
Yep, just picked up a 783 in .270 last night from Gander Mountain for $260 and it has a $40 rebate from Remington, so about $250 OTD. The trigger breaks very cleanly and I'm liking it a lot so far

There are many nice newer guns, but if you like nicely made older guns for under a thousand dollars you can find a pre-1964 Winchester Model 70. I myself prefer the feather weight version of this gun for it's lightness. It is both a collectable work of art and an extremely accurate tough and well made gun. It is by far my favorite gun just to hold in the hand and my go to for hunting deer.

Remington 783. It's on sale at Cabela's, Bass Pro, and Gander Mountain for $260 and is eligible for a $40 rebate from Remington until the end of the month IIRC. I just bought one last night (except chambered in .270, which I prefer for whitetail over 30-06) and the trigger breaks very nicely. It's not anything incredibly but it's a very good deer rifle and leaves you with plenty of money for good glass. I picked up the Nikon Buckmaster BDC 3x9-40 scope because it's on sale for $130 and its a pretty decent scope.

Rifle and scope for $360 before tax is a pretty damn good deal IMO. Let me know if you have any questions about the 783. I haven't received the scope yet from Cabela's so I don't have much to tell about it
Make sure whatever you get has a heavy barrel. Light barrels get hot quickly at a range.

Actually when it comes to Rocky Mountain Elk (800 lbs there about's) the 308 is a little on the short side. An animal that size needs a heavy ball for penetration. The max bullet weight for the .308 is 180 Grains. Oh yes you can load a heavier ball but your velocity gos to crap and your effective range drops. The 06 can use a 220 grain projectile with fair velocity. Personally I wouldn't go after Elk with any thing lighter than a .338. A Elk is a tough animal and I have seen just too many of them run off when hit by a .308 where the shooter didn't get precise bullet placement. The larger the projectile the bigger the window for bullet placement becomes.
